parameters.label: How much bitter compound is in the food
parameters.explain: Broccoli and Brussels sprouts contain bitter-tasting compounds; some foods have hardly any. This is a 0–10 teaching scale.

parameters.label: Her bitter-taste gene (TAS2R38)
parameters.explain: The twist dial: different versions of one gene, TAS2R38, help explain why the same food tastes much more bitter to some people. Switch Imani to her brother's version and see.

parameters.label: Salt on the broccoli
parameters.explain: Salt suppresses bitterness more than it suppresses other tastes — one reason food tastes better with a little salt.

parameters.label: Her nose
parameters.explain: Test the 'she has a cold' idea: a blocked nose makes food taste bland because flavour needs smell — but the tongue's bitter taste is still there.

parameters.label: Taste buds compared with average
parameters.explain: Supertasters may have more, or stronger, taste buds as well as sensitive receptors.

parameters.label: How the broccoli was cooked
parameters.explain: Test the 'cooked badly' idea: cooking changes the food a little for everyone at the table — it can't explain why only Imani finds it harsh.

explain.summary: Bitter taste starts when bitter compounds in food fit into bitter-taste receptors on the tongue. People inherit different versions of one receptor gene, TAS2R38, so the same broccoli sends a strong bitter signal in some people and a weak one in others. Imani has a sensitive version; her brother doesn't. Salt can dim bitterness, and a blocked nose dulls flavour but not bitterness.
rules: Bitterness rises with the amount of bitter compound in the food.
How strongly it rises depends on the version of the bitter-taste gene: non-taster, medium or supertaster.
More taste buds make the signal a little stronger.
A blocked nose lowers flavour from smell, but not the tongue's bitter taste.

source.fact: Different versions (alleles) of the bitter-receptor gene TAS2R38 are partly responsible for differences in how bitter people find things; people with more of the sensitive receptor rated a bitter test chemical as more intense.
About 25% of people in the U.S. are 'supertasters' of the bitter test chemical PROP, linked to the TAS2R38 gene; supertasters may have more or stronger taste buds, and they are born, not made.
Salt enhances flavour by suppressing bitterness: in experiments, salt suppressed bitterness much more than sweetness.
Taste cells detect at least five basic tastes, including bitter. Flavour is taste combined with a food's aroma, so a stuffed-up nose from a cold makes food taste bland.

choice.why: Real sensitivity is a range; three groups make the comparison between Imani and her brother clear. Supertasters are given 4 times the bitter signal of non-tasters.

choice.what: Salt cuts bitterness by up to about 45%
choice.why: Salt clearly suppresses bitterness; the exact amount depends on how much salt and which bitter compound.

choice.what: Taste-bud number has a small effect (±20%)
choice.why: Researchers still debate how much the number of taste buds matters compared with the receptor genes.

choice.what: A blocked nose only changes smell-based flavour
choice.why: Bitter is one of the tongue's basic tastes, so it is still detected when the nose is blocked.

illustrative: The 0–10 'bitter compound' and bitterness scales are teaching scales, not measurements.
How much cooking changes the bitter compounds is a made-up size: the point is that it changes the food for everyone at the table, not just for Imani.
provenance.studying: Scientists are still working out how all the different bitter-receptor genes (there are many besides TAS2R38) combine to shape what each person likes to eat.

citations.title: Human bitter perception correlates with bitter receptor messenger RNA expression in taste cells (Am J Clin Nutr)
citations.supports: Abstract: alleles of the TAS2R38 gene are responsible in part for variation in bitter taste perception; receptor expression varied widely and correlated with ratings of PROP bitterness and with diet.

citations.title: What It Means To Be a Supertaster
citations.supports: About 25% of people in the U.S. are PROP supertasters; this is due to the TAS2R38 gene; supertasters may have more or stronger taste buds; supertasters are born, not made; many vegetables taste bitter.

citations.title: Salt enhances flavour by suppressing bitterness (Nature 387, 563)
citations.supports: Breslin & Beauchamp: salts potentiate flavour through selective suppression of bitterness; the bitterness of urea was suppressed much more by salt than the sweetness of sucrose.

citations.title: Taste Disorders
citations.publisher: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders
citations.supports: Taste cells respond to at least five basic tastes including bitter; taste combines with aroma to make flavour; when your nose is stuffed up by a cold or flu, food can taste bland.

does: Shows the same food sending a different bitter signal depending on inherited taste genes
Shows that salt dims bitterness and a blocked nose dims flavour, not bitterness
Shows why cooking can't explain a difference between two people eating the same food
doesnt: Measure anyone's own taste genes — Imani is fictional
Include the many other bitter-taste genes, or how habits and culture shape what we like
Say anything about health or what anyone should eat
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If food suddenly starts tasting very different or strange to you, mention it to an adult.
